Our friend, colleague, and industry leader Rik Van Mol passed away peacefully last week with his family at his side. It was a shock to us all.

Rik dedicated his career to life sciences. He was a vital part of the industry and made a huge impact at Veeva in so many ways.

The world has lost an incredible human being far too early. Rik was a truly exceptional person in every way, bringing kindness, leadership, vision, energy, humor, style, and intuition to everything he did. He was an amazing leader and friend, a genuine inspiration, and such a gift to his family, Veeva, our customers, and the world.

For all of us who worked closely with Rik, there are no words to express the sorrow we feel. The outpouring of messages and calls over the last few days shows just how much he meant to everyone. I was privileged to work alongside Rik all these years. He will live on in my memory and remain a positive influence on me for all my days.

Our hearts go out to Rik’s family and to everyone who knew and loved him. Condolences can be shared with Rik’s family at https://lnkd.in/gjbKzHvt 

For those wishing to send flowers, Rik’s family prefers donations in his memory to Hartvereniging Aalst (HARVA vzw), a patient association for cardiovascular disease located at Lindenstraat 94B, 9300 Aalst, IBAN BE79 7805 6151 5633 with the note ‘Rik Van Mol’.

Rest in peace and thank you for everything Rik.

Great news! Non-competes are now illegal in Washington State! 

Thank you Governor Ferguson for having the courage to sign the bill into law last week. The new Washington law is very comprehensive like the long standing non-compete law in California.

This is a big win for employee freedom, innovation and the Washington State economy. I hope other states follow suit. Especially New York, where Governor Hochul, under pressure from big business, vetoed a bipartisan non-compete bill in December 2023.

Everybody knows that banning non-competes is good for workers, but is a non-compete ban good for the economy?  It sure is!  

Here is a simple example to illustrate the point.  Could OpenAI and Anthropic have started anywhere else in the U.S. other than California? No, because talent movement is restricted in most states and that makes all the difference when a movement is starting. Maybe the next big tech revolution can start in Washington!
 
Congratulations to Washington State!
 
 #noncompetes #leadership #innovation

posts.content:
AI is changing the enterprise technology landscape, with major implications for business leaders. Your enterprise technology architecture is no longer just infrastructure. It’s how work gets done, with agents actively taking on some tasks previously handled by humans.

This new way of working is enabled by a new technology architecture: Models, Agents, and Applications, the 𝗠𝗔𝗔𝗣 𝗔𝗿𝗰𝗵𝗶𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲.

𝗠𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀 are frontier models like Anthropic, OpenAI, or Gemini. They can reason, generate, and interpret. They understand the capabilities of your core applications and use that context in their reasoning.

𝗔𝗴𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 are a new type of knowledge worker. They use models for reasoning and applications for execution. Dedicated agents will take on some tasks that previously required humans.

𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 are your systems of record. They codify your industry’s business rules and your company’s operating model, providing the structure and consistency needed to run the business. Core applications are becoming "dual mode," controllable by both human users and agents. To enable this, applications must be easily understood by models and controllable by agents.

Your enterprise technology architecture is no longer just a technical decision. It reflects your operating model and your workforce. It’s about digital labor and the nature of work itself. CEOs need to take an active role and redefine how IT and the business work together in this new era. 

I’ll share more this week on how Veeva Systems is evolving at the application and agent layers to enable this transformation in life sciences.

#AI #EnterpriseTechnology #FutureOfWork #DigitalLabor #MAAP #EnterpriseArchitecture #LifeSciences #CEO

posts.content:
I know Veeva Systems versus Salesforce for life sciences CRM is of interest to many and there’s a lot of misinformation and hype out there. So, I wanted to share my view and some key facts.

Why do I write a post like this? It’s an important decision that can have a big impact. I care about the industry, our customers, and our employees. Having focused on industry specific technology at Veeva for 18 years now, after many years in horizontal technology at IBM, PeopleSoft, and Salesforce, I have gotten to see a lot.   

Veeva is the best choice for life sciences CRM because it is a deep application that is proven today with live customers from a trusted company committed to the industry. It is also the fastest path to AI that is useful and practical for biopharma field teams.

Salesforce is too risky and too expensive. Salesforce does not have a deep application, live customers, or track record of commitment to the industry.
So, Salesforce customers will have to customize too much and recreate too many essential capabilities that already exist in Vault CRM. That leads to long, expensive, poor quality, and risky projects and a redo some years down the road when business models change.

Customers should be careful about the motives of system integrators and other third parties in this decision. A more expensive, more custom project means more revenue for system integrators and other third parties, so that must be considered and managed effectively in the decision process.

To help provide clarity, I’ve included some important information in the table below. It represents the facts as I know them and I will likely update the table every few months or so over the coming year.

For more detail on Veeva versus Salesforce, why the facts below are important, and how I think this will play out and why, see my blog post https://lnkd.in/gsrAU3iq

posts.content:
Based on the feedback I received on my last post, it’s clear there is a lot of interest in the Veeva versus Salesforce debate.

I wanted to address one big and important misconception I heard, which is “either Salesforce or Veeva will work.” 
  
Global biopharma CRM programs are very hard to implement well. They failed a lot before Veeva made a great product that works around the globe and stayed with it for the industry for the long-term. CRM projects can still fail if the product and services are not right and without a partner with a commitment to customer success and the industry for the long haul. 

Salesforce has no customers live, no generally available product, and no services or consulting arm that knows how to do a global biopharma CRM program. So, the risk of failure is high. A difficult, long, costly implementation is almost certain. 

There is a higher chance of success with Salesforce if a company realizes they are choosing a mostly custom-build approach, fully staff for that, and invest sufficient resources over time to rebuild the core, keep up with changes, and also innovate. Not every company is able to do that or wants to allocate their strategic resources in that way.
 
And a custom system reflects the point in time it was built and the ideas of specific people on the project. This causes issues over time because companies then have a system that  becomes out of date as the market, environment, and people that built the system change. It will get redone by somebody at some point, so that’s another project.

That’s probably the last I will say about Salesforce for a while. I will have more next week on Veeva AI for Vault CRM!

posts.content:
I have long opposed the use of employment non-compete agreements as they are bad for employees and the economy. 

Yesterday's announcement of the FTC rule against non-competes is a step in the right direction, but it is not the same as a federal law. The FTC rule can be contested in court or changed as the administration changes. We continue to work toward a more durable solution, which would be a federal law banning employment non-compete agreements across the country.

Read more about non-competes in my January 2023 Medium post.  bit.ly/3iG7Otn
